title: Building a PhD Living-Cost Budget for the UK, Germany and the Netherlands
seoTitle: PhD Living Costs: UK, Germany and Netherlands
seoDescription: Build a PhD budget for the UK, Germany or Netherlands using take-home income, actual housing costs, moving expenses and clear assumptions.
intro: Compare offers using a monthly budget for the actual city. Start with take-home income, rent and insurance, then add moving costs, tuition gaps and the expenses that arrive before your first payment.
description:
Compare offers using a monthly budget for the actual city. Start with take-home income, rent and insurance, then add moving costs, tuition gaps and the expenses that arrive before your first payment.

Start with take-home income

Record the amount you expect to receive each month, not only the advertised annual payment. A gross salary may include deductions; a stipend can have different treatment. Confirm whether the payment covers the full year and whether tuition, insurance or other mandatory charges come out of it.

Build the budget for one city

List housing, utilities, food, transport, insurance, phone costs and essential study expenses. Use university accommodation information and current rental listings for the area where you would actually live. Check whether a rent quote includes bills and whether the contract requires payment during university holidays.

Use a range for uncertain costs and keep the assumptions visible. A room in shared accommodation and a private studio are different budgets. The same is true for a single researcher and someone moving with dependants.

Add the first-month costs

Deposits, temporary accommodation, travel, visa-related charges and basic household items can arrive before the first salary or stipend. Ask the host when payments begin and whether relocation support is available. Keep this initial cash requirement separate from the ordinary monthly budget.

Compare offers using the same categories

For a UK studentship, check fee status and whether the award covers an international tuition difference. For German employment, check the contract percentage and likely deductions. For Dutch employment, check the vacancy's salary progression and terms. These questions matter more than comparing a single national average.

Create three totals: expected monthly income, expected recurring expenses and initial moving costs. Then examine whether a modest increase in rent or an unexpected delay in payment would create a funding problem.

Recheck before accepting

Send the funding office any question that remains unclear, particularly on tuition, insurance and payment dates. Ask current researchers about accommodation options while treating personal budgets as examples rather than guarantees. Avoid publishing a set of invented 2027 prices: use dated sources and update the budget for the offer in front of you.

Build a budget with two totals

Use one total for normal monthly spending and another for the move. Monthly costs might include rent, bills, transport, food and insurance; the moving total might include travel, deposits and temporary accommodation. List tuition or compulsory fees separately if the award does not cover them. As a hypothetical example, an offer may look comfortable each month but require a deposit before its first payment. Ask when funding starts and whether relocation support exists. A small cash-flow timeline can identify that gap more clearly than an annual income figure.

Compare housing choices rather than national averages

Begin with the place where the laboratory or department is located. Then choose a realistic housing type and commuting area. A city-centre studio and a room in a shared house describe different decisions, even within the same university. Keep the rent quote, included bills and contract dates beside each estimate so that another person could understand how you reached the total.

Ask university accommodation services about current availability and use live listings to test the likely range. Asking current doctoral researchers can help identify practical issues such as transport or deposits, but a colleague's spending remains one person's example. Do not copy it into your budget without checking whether your household, insurance and housing needs are comparable.

A worked monthly budget with invented figures

Budget lineIllustrative monthly amountWhat to verify for a real offer
Spendable income2,100 local-currency unitsPayroll or award confirmation and funded months.
Rent and bills950 unitsContract, utilities, internet and any compulsory charges.
Food and household needs300 unitsYour household size and local prices.
Transport, phone and insurance200 unitsCommute, coverage and any amount already deducted from pay.
Remaining after these items650 unitsOther essential costs, savings and any uncovered study fees.

The arithmetic is 2,100 minus 950 minus 300 minus 200, leaving 650. These figures are deliberately hypothetical and are not quoted prices for the UK, Germany or the Netherlands. A table with transparent assumptions is more useful than a precise-looking national total assembled from unrelated years.

Test the budget when one assumption changes

If rent in that example were 150 units higher, the remaining amount would fall to 500. If the first payment arrived a month after you moved, you would also need money to cover the initial interval. These are different questions: ordinary monthly affordability and the cash required to start. Keep both visible rather than hiding startup costs inside an annual average.

For salaried positions, avoid deducting the same item twice. If insurance or another contribution is already included in the payroll estimate, record that fact before adding a separate monthly bill. For stipends, check what you must arrange independently. Ask the relevant office about your own arrangement rather than assuming all researchers have the same coverage.

Compare the full research period

Write down the guaranteed funding end date and any tuition support ending earlier. Keep a separate note for continuation fees and likely thesis-writing arrangements. A positive first-year budget does not establish that every later period is covered. Ask what is confirmed and what requires another award or contract.

Should I convert every offer into my home currency?

You can use a dated conversion for comparison, but build the living-cost budget in the currency you will spend. Exchange-rate changes should not be mistaken for changes in local affordability.

Should I include possible teaching income?

Keep it separate until the role, payment and permission to work are confirmed. A funding decision should remain understandable without relying on an uncertain job.

Official sources and further reading

Requirements and policies should be checked for your programme and application date. Sources checked on 19 October 2026.

  • UKRI: guidance for training grant holders
  • DAAD: doctoral finance

Related guides

  • Compare PhD Salaries and Stipends: Net Income, Fees and Living Costs
  • UK Student Visa Finances, ATAS and the Graduate Route Explained
  • TV-L E13 PhD Pay in Germany: Contract Percentage, Gross Pay and Benefits
